passage:
I'm Irfan, and at the funeral of my colleague Mehak's father last winter I nearly said something I'm glad I didn't. The old man had been famous in our office for his terrible puns, and one of them came into my head just as I stood in the queue to pay respects. It was genuinely funny, and it would have made everyone laugh.
Then I saw Mehak standing by the photograph, holding a folded shawl to her chest. Her eyes were red. I could see how the joke would land: loud, in a room full of people who couldn't laugh yet.
I said, "He was always so kind to me," and stood there. A month later, at the memorial, Mehak told the pun herself, and the room laughed with her, wet-eyed.

qa.q: What was the old man famous for in the office?
qa.a: He was famous for his terrible puns.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling as the pun came into his head in the queue?
qa.a: Irfan felt tempted, since the joke was funny, but then uneasy after seeing Mehak's red eyes.

qa.q: What did Irfan choose to say instead of the pun?
qa.a: Irfan said that the old man had always been kind, and stood quietly. It gave comfort without hurting anyone.

qa.q: How might Mehak have felt when she saw the room laugh with her at the memorial?
qa.a: Mehak was probably comforted, sad and glad together, since the laughter was hers to invite. It honoured her father instead of hurting her.

grounding: A person holds back a joke at a funeral because the timing would wound, and sees it land later when the family invites it.

Supervisor's note about Vidya, Sales.
On Thursday, Tarun's presentation to the regional client stalled when the demo failed twice, and the client left early. Tarun looked pale and stared at his laptop.
In the corridor afterwards, a colleague said, "Well, that was a disaster, wasn't it?" and laughed. I saw Vidya, who has a real gift for quick jokes, start to say something, then close her mouth. She stood near Tarun for a minute, then said quietly, "Want a tea? I'll walk down with you."
Two weeks later, at the review meeting, Tarun himself told the story of the frozen demo as a funny one. Vidya laughed with him. I noted her timing. The joke waited until he made it, and it was his to tell.

qa.q: On which day did Tarun's demo fail?
qa.a: Tarun's demo failed on Thursday.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling when she began to say something and then closed her mouth?
qa.a: Vidya probably felt the pull of a joke but also sensed Tarun was hurting, so she held it back to protect him.

qa.q: What did Vidya do instead of joking in the corridor?
qa.a: Vidya stayed near Tarun and offered to walk down for tea with him. That gave him company without pressure.

qa.q: How might Tarun have felt when the colleague laughed about the disaster?
qa.a: Tarun was probably hurt and embarrassed, already pale and staring at the laptop, so the laugh would have stung.

grounding: A person notices a joke straight after someone's fresh failure would wound, holds it, and lets the person tell it later.

passage:
Thursday, very late.
Today was the condolence visit at Jatin's house for his father. The room was full of white clothes and quiet voices. Jatin sat on the mattress by the photo, very straight, not crying.
Then his uncle mentioned the scooter, and I remembered the time Jatin's father drove his scooter into the Ganesh pandal and came out with a garland round his neck. It's the funniest story I know. It was right on my tongue. I actually opened my mouth.
Then I looked at Jatin's face. It was grey. His hands were gripping his knees. I closed my mouth and just sat next to him, shoulder to shoulder, for an hour.
Maybe one day he'll tell that story himself and we'll laugh. That has to be his choice, not mine.
Chaitanya

qa.q: What did Jatin's father drive into?
qa.a: He drove his scooter into the Ganesh pandal.

qa.a: Chaitanya felt a tug of concern and caution, seeing Jatin's grey face and gripping hands, and sensed the story would hurt him.

qa.a: Chaitanya sat next to Jatin, shoulder to shoulder, for an hour, offering quiet company when a joke could have wounded.

qa.a: He may need people to sit with him and let him decide when, or whether, to laugh about his father's stories.

passage: At the Moga cattle fair, Jasleen's new tractor got stuck in the mud right in front of the judges' stand. She revved it, the wheels spun, and a wave of brown water hit the front row. Half the fair turned to look. Some boys by the tea stall started laughing. Shankar, standing near the gate with his uncle, had the perfect line ready. Something about Jasleen entering the tractor in the buffalo race. He'd have gotten a big laugh. Then he saw her face as she climbed down. Her ears were red. She'd saved for two years for that tractor, and everyone in the village knew it. Shankar swallowed the joke. He walked over, rolled up his trousers and said, "Push on three?" Four other men joined him. The tractor came free on the second push.

qa.q: Where did Jasleen's tractor get stuck?
qa.a: In the mud right in front of the judges' stand.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling when he saw Jasleen's red ears?
qa.a: Shankar felt a pang of sympathy and caution, sensing that his joke would wound her in front of the whole fair.

qa.q: What would you advise someone who has a funny line ready at a moment like this?
qa.a: Look at the person's face first; if they're hurting, save the joke and offer help, like Shankar did.

qa.q: What was it like for Jasleen when the boys laughed?
qa.a: She was probably humiliated, having saved for two years and now failing publicly in front of the village.

grounding: Shows a person noticing that a joke about a fresh public failure would wound, holding it and helping instead.

passage: Pablo climbed the four flights to Nadia's flat in Valencia with a bag of oranges and a joke ready. All week they had teased each other about the conservatory audition panel, three stern judges they called "the owls", and he had a good one about owls. Nadia opened the door in yesterday's sweater. The cello case sat closed by the sofa, and a letter lay face down on the table. "They said no," she said flatly. Pablo felt the owl joke right at the front of his mouth. He looked at the letter, then at her red eyes, and swallowed it. "I'm sorry," he said instead, and started peeling an orange for her. Two weeks later, when she was laughing about the audition herself, he finally told it. She laughed so hard she snorted.

qa.q: What did Pablo bring to Nadia's flat?
qa.a: He brought a bag of oranges.

qa.a: He felt the urge to lighten things but also uneasy, sensing from her red eyes and the face-down letter that the joke would hurt.

qa.q: When did the joke finally work, and why?
qa.a: Two weeks later, when Nadia was already laughing about the audition herself, so the joke joined her mood instead of mocking her pain.

qa.q: What might Nadia have felt if Pablo had told the joke at the door?
qa.a: She might have felt hurt and unseen, as if her rejection were just material for a laugh.
